title: Beige Book — March 5, 2025
html:
Official report: Summary · Full PDF Local PDF: 2025-03-05 Beige Book.pdf

Overall economic activity

Activity rose slightly since mid-January. Six Districts reported no change, four reported modest or moderate growth, and two reported slight contractions. Manufacturing posted slight to modest gains in most Districts, while residential and nonresidential construction fell modestly. Residential real estate was mixed, with continuing inventory shortages. Agriculture deteriorated somewhat, and banking activity was slightly higher on balance. Expectations for the months ahead were slightly optimistic. The report was prepared by the Minneapolis Fed.

Consumer spending

Spending was lower on balance. Demand for essentials held up, but lower-income shoppers became more price-sensitive on discretionary purchases. Unusual weather hurt leisure and hospitality, and vehicle sales were modestly lower.

Labor markets

Employment nudged up: four Districts reported slight gains, seven no change and one a slight decline. Health care and finance added jobs; manufacturing and information technology lost some. Labor availability improved in many sectors, though some occupations stayed tight. Uncertainty about immigration and other issues was affecting labor demand. Wage growth was modest to moderate, slightly slower than before.

Prices

Prices rose moderately in most Districts, and several saw the pace pick up. "Input price pressures were generally greater than sales price pressures," especially in manufacturing and construction, and many firms struggled to pass costs along. Eggs and other food ingredients, insurance and freight costs rose notably. Most contacts expected potential tariffs on inputs to push their prices up; a few raised prices preemptively.

Notable themes

  • Tariffs/trade policy: Concern spanned manufacturers from petrochemicals to office equipment; builders worried about tariffs raising lumber and material costs.
  • Uncertainty: Rising, particularly around trade and immigration.
  • Consumer stress: Lower-income households pulling back on discretionary spending.
  • Housing: Inventory shortages persisted.

District highlights

  • Boston: A surge in home sales helped activity.
  • New York: Selling-price increases picked up to a moderate pace; labor supply and demand back in balance.
  • Philadelphia: Fiscal and trade policy changes seen as an inflation risk.
  • St. Louis: Prices rose more than expected; firms delayed investment; outlook fell from slightly optimistic to neutral.
  • Kansas City: Consumer spending fell moderately.
  • Dallas: Moderate expansion and notably stronger lending, but uncertainty rose sharply.
  • San Francisco: Activity ticked down.

Read-through for SPY

  • Growth was still positive but consumer spending, the economy's main engine, softened.
  • Input costs outrunning selling prices pointed to possible margin pressure for companies.
  • Tariff-driven price expectations and rising uncertainty were a headwind for sentiment and could complicate rate cuts.
